candidates.context: This guidance addresses withdrawable volume and labeled vial fill size for injectable drug 28 products that are packaged in vials and ampules, including products that require reconstitution. 29 It does not address injectable drug products in other packaging types (e.g., prefilled syringe 30 package systems and intravenous infusion bags) or noninjectable products, because there may be 31 unique considerations for these packaging configurations. The recommendations in this 32 guidance apply to new drug applications (NDAs), abbreviated new drug applications (ANDAs), 33 biologics license applications (BLAs), as well as supplements or other changes to these 34 applications for new packaging or other changes that may affect the fill volume. 35 1 The term vial used throughout this guidance refers to both vial and ampule package types.

candidates.statement: The United States Pharmacopeia (USP) General Chapter <1> Injections provides that each 56 container of an injectable product is filled with a volume that slightly exceeds the content 57 indicated in the labeling. 6 The excess volumes are meant to be sufficient to permit withdrawal 58 and administration of the labeled volumes. FDA regulations at 21 CFR 201.51(g) provide that 59 for drugs in ampules or vials that are intended for injection, the declaration of net quantity of 60 contents on the label is considered to express the minimum quantity of contents and further 61 requires that variation above the stated measure must comply with the excess volumes set forth 62 in USP. USP General Chapter <1151> Pharmaceutical Dosage Forms provides excess volume 63 recommendations for mobile and viscous liquids in a range of fill volumes, noting that the excess 64 volumes recommended are usually sufficient to permit withdrawal and administration of the 65 labeled volumes. Allowable excess volume may also be referred to as “overfill,” but should not 66 be confused with “overage,” which is addressed in a separate guidance. 7 Generally, an applicant 67 should not declare the amount of overfill on the container label. 68
candidates.context: A. Allowable Excess Volume 54 4 Perz J, Thompson N, Schaefer M, Patel P, 2010, US Outbreak Investigations Highlight the Need for Safe Injection Practices and Basic Infection Control, Clinics in Liver Disease, 14:137-151.

candidates.statement: 6 For a drug product for which there is an official USP drug product monograph, the product must comply with the standards set forth therein, including the standards set forth in General Chapter <1>, unless expressly excepted in that drug product monograph. See Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, sections 501(b) (21 U.S.C. 351(b)) and 502(g) (21 U.S.C. 352(g)); USP 37-NF 32, General Notices and Requirements 2.10. Official Text. Thus, for an injectable drug product for which a USP monograph exists and incorporates General Chapter <1>, the provision regarding inclusion of a slight volume exceeding the labeled volume is a mandatory requirement; for injectable products without a USP monograph that incorporates General Chapter <1>, compliance with the slight excess volume provision is strongly recommended. USP has proposed moving the text discussing the container content from USP General Chapter <1> Injections to USP General Chapter <697> Container Content for Injections. These proposed changes are being considered for USP 38.
candidates.context: 5 Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Injection Safety, Safe Injection Practices to Prevent Transmission of Infections to Patients, 2007 Guideline for Isolation Precautions: Preventing Transmission of Infectious Agents in Healthcare Settings (http://www.cdc.gov/injectionsafety/IP07_standardPrecaution.html). 7 Overage is an amount of a drug substance in excess of the label claim. The use of an overage to compensate for degradation during manufacture or a product’s shelf life, or to extend the shelf life is generally discouraged. The use of an overage is discussed in section 2.2.2 of the International Conference on Harmonisation (ICH ), Guidance for Industry, Q8(R2) Pharmaceutical Development .

candidates.statement: While dosing flexibility is necessary with injectable drug products, applicants should determine 77 the appropriate vial fill sizes during product development, considering how the vials are likely to 78 be used. For example, single-dose vials are designed for use in a single patient as a single 79 injection/infusion. However, even when appropriately labeled, single-dose vials that contain 80 significantly 8 more drug than is required for a single dose may result in the misuse of the leftover 81 drug product. Similarly, the need to combine several single-dose vials for a single patient dose 82 may lead to medication errors and microbial contamination. 83
candidates.context: B. Labeled Vial Fill Size 75 According to USP General Chapter <1>, multiple-dose vials have a maximum container volume 85 sufficient to permit the withdrawal of not more than a total of 30 mL, unless otherwise specified 86 in the USP drug product monograph. 9 , 10 Setting a maximum volume in multiple-dose vials will 87 minimize vial septum punctures, which will reduce the risk of compromising vial integrity and 88 the potential for vial contamination. 89

candidates.statement: With respect to allowable excess volume, the applicant of drugs in ampules or vials intended for 93 injection must follow the requirements in 21 CFR 201.51(g). The regulation requires an 94 applicant to comply with the excess volume recommendations prescribed by the USP. 95 Therefore, for drugs in ampules and vials intended for injection, the applicant must comply with 96 the excess volume recommendations that appear in USP General Chapter <1151>. 11 In the case 97 of drug products requiring reconstitution, the product should be designed to meet the label claim 98 and acceptable overfill, and allow for correct dosing. Deviations from the recommendations in 99 USP General Chapter <1151> with regard to excess volume should be justified. 12 FDA 100 recommends providing the justification by obtaining extractable content testing data, which is 101
candidates.context: IV. DISCUSSION AND RECOMMENDATIONS 91 8 While it is not possible to specify a quantitative volume of remaining drug product that would generally be considered significant, volumes remaining that could provide a second dose, or would encourage pooling for a second dose, would be considered excessive.

candidates.statement: 10 For products without a USP monograph, multiple-dose vials must have a maximum fill volume sufficient to permit the withdrawal of not more than 30 mL, unless justified in the application.
candidates.context: 9 USP has proposed moving the text discussing the maximum container volume for multiple-dose vials from USP General Chapter <1> Injections to USP General Chapter <659> Packaging and Storage Requirements. These proposed changes are being considered for USP 38. 11 Typically, USP General Chapters titled with numbers above <1000> are considered to be recommendations and not requirements, unless the chapter is cited in a product-specific monograph or another General Chapter titled with a number below <1000>. However, in this case, because FDA’s regulations specifically require adherence to the USP recommendations on this topic, the recommendations in USP General Chapter <1151> are considered to be requirements.
